decisions.quote: Summary of Replication Attempt Based on the a priori criterion, the replication was not successful. However, the effect was close to significance (p = .086) and the effect sizes was not significantly different from the original effect. At the same time, the other main finding of the paper (power ratings are correlated with profits) was significant (p = .01). To a certain extent, the original choice of the a priori criterion was arbitrary because neither correlation was held up by the original authors as “the” important correlation.
decisions.location: primary report 76 (Rule & Ambady, 2008), Discussion, view line 818
decisions.reason: Resolving the dependent identity and competing_supported_matches flag first: although the RPP summary spreadsheet (Study Num 82, view line 1149) misprinted the journal citation metadata from Rule & Ambady's other 2008 paper in JPSP (an unclaimed/uncompleted entry at Study Num 83, view line 1150), the actual completed primary replication report (primary_report_index 76, view lines 809-820) explicitly tests Rule, N. O., & Ambady, N. (2008), 'The face of success: Inferences from chief executive officers' appearance predict company profits', Psychological Science, 19(2), 109-111 (DOI 10.1111/j.1467-9280.2008.02054.x), matching both shipped row 1896 and blind target 51. On the outcome, the pre-specified central confirmatory test (partial correlation between leadership ratings and company profits controlling for age, affect, and attractiveness) did not reach significance, r(41) = .27, p = .086, and both the Confirmatory Analysis and Summary of Replication Attempt explicitly conclude that 'Based on the a priori criterion, the replication was not successful' (consistent with Replicate (R) = no in the master dataset), despite a significant secondary correlation for power ratings (r(41) = .37, p = .01) and commentary noting consistency in direction. Both shipped and blind code 'failed'.

decisions.quote: Replication of Study The Face of Success by Rule & Ambady (2008, Psychological Science) Casey Eggleston cm5hv@virginia.edu Minha Lee mhl5b@virginia.edu Thomas Talhelm tat8dc@virginia.edu Introduction Rule and Ambady (2008) found that naïve college undergraduates’ impressions of Fortune 500 CEOs’ appearance correlated with company profits. CEOs they rated as appearing more powerful and looking like good leaders ran companies with higher profits. We chose the correlation between leadership and profits as our a priori criterion of successful replication.
decisions.location: primary report 76 (Rule & Ambady, 2008), Title and Introduction, view line 809
decisions.reason: Having resolved the tested original identity to Rule & Ambady (2008, Psychological Science, 19(2), 109-111; DOI 10.1111/j.1467-9280.2008.02054.x) as opposed to the uncompleted JPSP entry in the project spreadsheet, primary report 76 collected new student rater samples at the University of Virginia (142 for trait ratings, 145 for leadership ratings, and 68 for attractiveness ratings) using the original CEO face stimuli to test the original empirical hypothesis. This is a direct empirical replication ('replication').

decisions.quote: In conclusion, the present study was not able replicate the results of Study 4 of Dessalegn and Landau (2008). Nevertheless, the patterns in the data, together with other information that has emerged about the effect (Dessalegn and Landau, 2013) support the possibility that language may play a role in feature binding and object representation in memory. Ascertaining the size of this effect, its generality, and timing would require, however, larger and well characterized samples.
decisions.location: primary report 3 (Dessalegn & Landau, 2008), Discussion, view lines 126-127
decisions.reason: Primary report 3 (testing Study 4 of Dessalegn & Landau, 2008, DOI 10.1111/j.1467-9280.2008.02066.x) tested a single confirmatory effect: the two-group comparison between the directional and relational conditions on the proportion of match selections. That confirmatory test was statistically non-significant, t(45) = 1.534, p = .132, Cohen's d = .48. Although the author remarks in the opening of the Discussion that 'The present study provides a partial replication of their findings. Specifically, while replicating the direction of the effect, we failed to replicate its size and significance even though the present study had greater power,' under the codebook a single non-significant confirmatory result in the expected direction is not 'mixed' (which applies when multiple tested findings partly replicate and partly fail), and the exploratory post-hoc exclusion of two children (p = .036) does not govern the confirmatory replication verdict. The author explicitly states in the Commentary ('our failure to replicate the original result') and in the concluding overall verdict ('In conclusion, the present study was not able replicate the results of Study 4 of Dessalegn and Landau (2008)'), matching Replicate (R) = no in the RPP master dataset. Thus blind's coding of 'failed' is right.

decisions.quote: Janssen, N., Alario, F. X., & Caramazza, A. (2008). A word-order constraint on phonological activation. Psychological Science, 19(3), 216-220.
decisions.location: primary report 72 (Janssen, Alario, & Caramazza, 2008), References, view line 792
decisions.reason: Addressing the same_author_year_siblings flag: first author Niels Janssen (with senior author Alfonso Caramazza) has two distinct 2008 papers replicated in the RPP corpus—Janssen, Schirm, Mahon, & Caramazza (2008, JEP:LMC, DOI 10.1037/0278-7393.34.1.249; shipped row 1677 / blind target 21) and Janssen, Alario, & Caramazza (2008, Psychological Science, 19(3), 216-220, DOI 10.1111/j.1467-9280.2008.02070.x; shipped row 1905 / blind target 87). Primary report 72 explicitly replicates Experiment 2 of Janssen, Alario, & Caramazza (2008), confirming shipped row 1905's DOI '10.1111/j.1467-9280.2008.02070.x' and pairing with blind target 87.

decisions.quote: Following the results of Janssen et al (2008) Experiment 2, in this replication we expected to find no effect of congruency in the color naming task but a significant effect of congruency in the object naming task. The results of this experiment failed to replicate Janssen et al (2008), Experiment 2. In both tasks, we found that naming was numerically faster in congruent compared to incongruent trials. Although our results trended in the expected direction, they did not reach statistical significance.
decisions.location: primary report 72 (Janssen, Alario, & Caramazza, 2008), Discussion, view line 789
decisions.reason: In primary report 72 (testing Experiment 2 of Janssen, Alario, & Caramazza, 2008), the focal phonological congruency effect in the English object-naming task was non-significant in both the by-subjects analysis (t1(11) = 1.9, p = .09, dz = .54) and the by-items analysis (t2(39) = 0.9, p = .352, dz = .15). Under 'Summary of Replication Attempt', the author states the explicit overall verdict: 'The results of this experiment failed to replicate Janssen et al (2008), Experiment 2.' Although the Commentary later speculates that 'the small sample tested here and the failure to observe any congruency effect may suggest that this replication was underpowered' (even though N = 24 exceeded the a priori 95% power target of N = 22), the author's clear overall verdict in the Summary of Replication Attempt governs under Rule 1 of the codebook. Both shipped and blind code 'failed'.

decisions.quote: In this replication of Janssen et al. (2008), we sought to exactly reproduce the methodology used in the original paper. As the present work was conducted as part of the Reproducibility Project: Psychology, which asks volunteers to replicate the final experiment in their chosen paper, this is a direct replication of Experiment 2, which concerns English.
decisions.location: primary report 72 (Janssen, Alario, & Caramazza, 2008), Introduction, view line 784
decisions.reason: Primary report 72 collected new experimental data from 24 native English-speaking psychology students at the University of Dundee performing the object-naming and color-naming tasks to directly re-test Experiment 2 of Janssen, Alario, & Caramazza (2008). Both shipped and blind rightly classify the study type as 'replication'.
